newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry slams Kohl's planned tax reform.
newsitem.headline: German industry slams Kohl's planned tax reform.

text.p: German business leaders on Saturday severely criticised Chancellor Helmut Kohl's plan to reform the tax system, saying it would increase the tax burden on industry and drive even more jobs abroad.

The government sees the bill as a key structural reform which it says will reduce the notoriously high tax burden on companies in Germany, giving them an incentive to invest here and creating more jobs at home.

But in a report released ahead of publication on Monday, Spiegel news magazine quoted several German industrial leaders criticising the bill, which is due to go before the German lower house of parliament on Thursday.

The BDI German industry federation said in a statement recent amendments to the reform were not acceptable and warned Bonn that if it went ahead with such measures even more jobs in German industry would be "exported" to other countries.

"If Bonn decides to go ahead with plans that mean industry has a bigger rather than a smaller tax burden, then there is going to be trouble," the magazine quoted Hans Peter Stihl, head of the Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), as saying.

The news magazine also quoted BASF chairman Juergen Strube as saying "he had the impression Kohl's government had lost control" and that if it went ahead with the reform in its current form "no one would be want to invest in Germany".

The reforms aim to lower tax rates for companies and individuals while making it more difficult to avoid taxes and were originally intended to reduce the overall tax burden by 30 billion marks in 1999.

But it is still unclear if they will achieve that goal with the amendments, which were hammered out by Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats, Christian Social Union and Free Democrats to fill new gaps that emerged in the 1998 and 1999 budgets.

Bonn is struggling to whip its finances into shape in 1997, the crunch year for fulfilling the financial criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU). But its economic data for 1998 are also an important factor in deciding whether it will qualify to join the planned launch of EMU in 1999.
The amendments to the bill include provisions preventing firms from using profits to offset future losses and other tax alterations for companies.

In a statement issued late on Friday, the BDI said it was shocked that the Bonn coalition had ignored all its suggestions and warnings and was bulldozing ahead with the bill regardless of the burden it would create on industry.

"The decisions to counter-finance the tax reform of 1998 and 1999 as well as proposals for closing budget gaps are one-sided and unacceptable for industry in their current form," the BDI statement said.

But the leader of Kohl's junior coalition partner the FDP, Wolfgang Gerhard, said in an interview that he was satisfied with the tax bill, saying it was long overdue and was key to boosting Germany's depressed jobs market.

"This is an important incentive for jobs in Germany. We are doing something which other countries have long practised, we are unfortunately late. We could have done it sooner," Gerhard told Germany's N-TV all-news televison station on Saturday.
